object.medium: Tempera on mud-and-lime plaster over rock
object.description: The Bodhisattva Padmapani, 'he who holds the lotus', painted beside the shrine door of Cave 1 at Ajanta in the last decades of the fifth century. He stands over life size, his body swaying in a gentle curve, a blue lotus in his right hand, eyes half closed, surrounded by a crowd of smaller figures: attendants, a dark-skinned guard, musicians and animals. Ajanta is a horseshoe of thirty Buddhist monasteries and prayer halls cut into a cliff above a river gorge in the Deccan. The earliest date from the second century BCE; the great painted caves, including this one, were made in a single burst of patronage under the Vakataka king Harisena around 460 to 480 CE, then abandoned and forgotten in the jungle until a British hunting party found them in 1819. The paintings are tempera on a thin plaster of mud, lime and rice husk, and are the oldest surviving body of Indian painting. Padmapani is the single most reproduced image from them and has shaped how Indian art is pictured ever since.
facts: Cave 1 was probably sponsored by the Vakataka emperor Harisena and was never formally consecrated: there is no lamp-soot on the shrine image.
Padmapani and his pair Vajrapani flank the entrance to the Buddha shrine on the rear wall; both are over life size.
The pigments are earth colours plus lapis lazuli blue imported from Afghanistan.
The caves were lost to the forest for roughly a thousand years before their rediscovery in 1819.
